ImageDescription.value: A Peugeot 504 convertible series 1, designed and built in collaboration with the Turin-based coachbuilder Pininfarina. Here it is equipped with Dunlop rims. After having practiced discreet elegance on its 203, 403 and 404 with special bodies, Peugeot broke the mold in 1969. By clearly moving away from the 504 sedan, the new Sochalian coupes and convertibles finally dared the sexy touch, thus giving birth to one of the most beautiful cars of the erotic year. The Peugeot 504 is a logical, but above all necessary, evolution of the 404. Heckled by the Citroën ID and DS, the Renault 16 and even a more modern Simca 1500, this one quickly lost the superb quality that we knew from its debut in 1961 and 1962. Still young to be replaced, the 404 will be supported in September 1968 by a little big sister: a model designed to be its replacement but with whom she will live together for around ten years. Following the logic of gentrification which dictates the evolution of the brand's vehicles, the 504 rose into the 10, then 11 CV category (the 404 is a 9 CV) while retaining the same engine base as the 404, at namely an in-line four-cylinder overturned engine with hemispherical combustion chambers.

ImageDescription.value: A Peugeot 504 pickup Popemobile specially outfitted for Pope John Paul II’s apostolic journeys to the Paris region and Lisieux in May–June 1980, Lyon in 1986, and Alsace-Lorraine/Strasbourg in 1988. It is now on display at the Musée de l’Aventure Peugeot in Sochaux.

ImageDescription.value: Peugeot 504 Pickup – Pope John Paul II's Popemobile – at the Peugeot Museum in Sochaux. Based on a rugged 504 pickup, it was used during John Paul II's official trips to France—notably in May–June 1980 (Paris and Lisieux)—as well as during visits to Lyon in 1986 and Alsace-Lorraine/Strasbourg in 1988.
